body: Out of curiosity, how is this table generated? There could be a comment above it to explain this.
This is simply sizes for each block by index. Each subsequent one after 1024 increases by 1.5 times. I don't know if it makes sense to document it.
In case the string is already a stringname, this variable is not used. I'd rather have either 2 calls to push_callp in the two branches of the if, or use a ternary operator for the second parameter.

Just a note: if a plain mutex is faster than a spinlock, it means the locked code doesn't respect some fundamental requirement of critical sections -- and usually loops don't. Certainly, loops involving a call *do not* (a mutex should never be locked across a same-level-or-above-logic call).

However, changing this may require a deep redesign of the data structure and the logic in order to be more MT-friendly.

A no-no of having mutex locked is when you enter a system call, like memfree.
it would be better to allocate a stack vector with the blocks to be removed, unlock, then call memfree on the removed blocks.

I don't think this is a correct implementation of a RWLock.
0) There is an initialisation race, which is silently dealt by crashing or deadlocking the system.
1) multiple readers could deadlock each-other, if they happen to have the same get_thread_pos(), which is very possible in many scenarios.
2) readers could starve the writer; in properly written rwlock, once a writer comes in, all other readers incoming are put to wait, and as the last reader exits the writer achieve the lock. Here, the readers can easily starve the writer, and a set of readers that was randomly blocked out before the writers came in.
Suppose we have 5 locks.
Writer locks N0, 1 and 2.
Now reader with slot 3 starts starving, locking and unlocking in a tight loop. There is no guarantee of fairness for mutexes (and if BinaryMutex is, it shouldn't: unfairness it's a feature, not a bug), so the writer can be locked forever. Now, if R0-2 come in, they will be locked -- while other readers are allowed to proceed.
3) locking multiple mutexes is very often a bad idea, and it can cause multiple contexts switches. On modern architectures, with tens of cores and hundreds of threads, this hurts a lot.
4) std::shared_mutex implements this functionality correctly, as efficiently as theoretically possible and is "peer reviewed" at academic level. I don't see why we shouldn't use it.
